title: The Nuggets’ Troubling Start
contentHtml:
We should be wary of overreacting to the first week of the NBA season, and of overindexing its importance in evaluating teams. It’s a natural tendency. This is the first real NBA basketball we’ve seen in months, and we have caveman brains that fall victim to recency bias.

And it took only six days for injuries to puncture a giant hole in the Oklahoma City Thunder, upending the championship race before it could even begin. (For more on that, check out Monday’s episode of The Zach Lowe Show!) The landscape is ever-changing.

So it’s too early to panic about the Denver Nuggets’ 1-2 start. Cameron Johnson, oft injured, played 11 minutes in Denver’s season-opening loss to the Thunder before getting injured again. Spencer Jones hasn’t played at all because of a hamstring issue. Julian Strawther is hurt, but Strawther Straits is pretty lifeless these days even when its namesake does suit up. Aaron Gordon seems to have lost some dynamism. (It’s early!)

But the Nuggets, proud champions, have opened the season with two double-digit losses—including to the previously winless Golden State Warriors on Monday night—and a miracle home comeback win against the New Orleans Pelicans, whose lineups made no sense amid an embarrassing, turnover-addled collapse in crunch time. The home fans booed Denver in that game, and Nikola Jokic responded afterward by claiming that those fans were no longer welcome at home games. Good times!

It’s probably not a great sign that Trevon Brazile, a rookie second-round pick, feels immediately essential as someone with athletic pop who also might be able to hit an open 3. With Gordon’s leaping a little muted compared to his glory days—he was indeed robbed of at least one win in the Kia Sprite Taco Bell Verizon Poulan Weed-Eater Slam Dunk Contest, sponsored by Pop-Tarts—Denver is desperate for any ounce of oomph and verticality. As Yaxel Lendeborg trampled over everyone in Denver on Monday, the Nuggets too often looked simply like the less talented team—while playing a squad that will be lucky to make the play-in tournament.

Through three games, Denver is 18th in offense and 26th on defense. The latter number is not a surprise, although the Nuggets obviously have to at least sniff league average on defense if they want to compete. They have looked defeated, dispirited, helpless whenever opponents get near the basket. That includes Jokic. There have been too many hiccups of miscommunication and uncontested opponent run-outs—stuff they should at least mitigate as they get settled.

The offense has normalized after Oklahoma City smothered Denver in the opener, but there are worrisome signs under the hood—trends that good teamwide health alone may not be able to correct.
